passed.title: LazyFrame.update without `on` aligns rows by position and skips nulls
passed.trap: If `on` is omitted, `LazyFrame.update` joins on the *implicit row index*. Row 0 of `other` overwrites row 0 of the frame, key columns included, so an update meant to go by key is silently applied to the wrong rows. Nulls in `other` are also ignored by default (`include_nulls=False`), so you cannot clear a value unless you pass `include_nulls=True`. Always pass `on=` (or `left_on`/`right_on`). The API is marked unstable.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [10, 20, 30]})
new = pl.LazyFrame({"A": [2, 3], "B": [None, 99]})

# Wrong: no `on`, so rows are matched by position and column A is overwritten too
print(lf.update(new).collect().to_dicts())

# Right: match on the key; the null in `new` is ignored by default
print(lf.update(new, on="A").collect().to_dicts())

# To write the null through, opt in explicitly
print(lf.update(new, on="A", include_nulls=True).collect().to_dicts())

passed.title: LazyFrame.unique keeps an arbitrary duplicate in arbitrary order by default
passed.trap: pandas `drop_duplicates` keeps the first row and preserves order. `LazyFrame.unique` defaults to `keep='any'` and `maintain_order=False`, which guarantee neither which duplicate survives nor the output order. Pass `keep='first'` (or `'last'`) and `maintain_order=True` when either matters. pandas `keep=False` corresponds to `keep='none'`, which drops every duplicated row.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"id": [1, 2, 1], "v": ["a", "b", "c"]})

# Default: only the row count is guaranteed, not which `v` is kept for id=1
print(lf.unique(subset="id").collect().height)

# pandas-like: keep the first occurrence, in original order
print(lf.unique(subset="id", keep="first", maintain_order=True).collect().to_dicts())

# pandas keep=False equivalent: drop every duplicated key
print(lf.unique(subset="id", keep="none").collect().to_dicts())

passed.title: LazyFrame.sort puts nulls first and is not stable by default
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.sort` defaults to `nulls_last=False`, so nulls come *first*, even when `descending=True`. pandas habits expect missing values at the end. Ties are also not guaranteed to keep their input order unless `maintain_order=True`. Pass `nulls_last=True` and/or `maintain_order=True` explicitly when the order of nulls or ties matters.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [2, None, 1]})
print(lf.sort("a").collect().get_column("a").to_list())
print(lf.sort("a", descending=True).collect().get_column("a").to_list())
print(lf.sort("a", nulls_last=True).collect().get_column("a").to_list())

ties = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [1, 1, 0], "v": ["first", "second", "third"]})
# Stable sort: tied rows keep their input order
print(ties.sort("k", maintain_order=True).collect().get_column("v").to_list())

passed.title: LazyFrame.top_k output is unordered and uses `reverse`, not `descending`
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.top_k` returns the k largest rows in no particular order. Do not assume row 0 is the maximum; chain `LazyFrame.sort` if order matters. Since 1.0.0 the direction flag is `reverse` (renamed from `descending`), and `reverse=True` selects the k *smallest* rows. Non-null values are always preferred over nulls, whichever direction you use.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"name": ["a", "b", "c", "d"], "score": [3, None, 5, 1]})

# Largest two, then sorted explicitly because top_k does not order its output
print(lf.top_k(2, by="score").sort("score", descending=True).collect().to_dicts())

# Smallest two: reverse=True; the null is still not picked
print(lf.top_k(2, by="score", reverse=True).sort("score").collect().to_dicts())

passed.title: Replace deprecated LazyFrame.with_context with a horizontal pl.concat
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.with_context` is deprecated since 1.0.0. Use `pl.concat([...], how='horizontal')` to bring another frame's columns into scope. Rename the other frame's columns first (for example with `Expr.name.suffix`) so they do not collide with yours. Then compute aggregates such as `Expr.median` on the borrowed columns.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

train = pl.LazyFrame({"x": [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]})
test = pl.LazyFrame({"x": [-1.0, None, 5.0]})

both = pl.concat(
    [test, train.select(pl.all().name.suffix("_train"))], how="horizontal"
)
out = both.select(pl.col("x").fill_null(pl.col("x_train").median()))
print(out.collect().to_dicts())

passed.title: LazyFrame.std and var default to sample statistics (ddof=1), unlike numpy
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.std` and `LazyFrame.var` divide by N - 1 by default (`ddof=1`). That matches pandas but not numpy, whose default is population statistics (`ddof=0`). Porting numpy code without passing `ddof=0` silently changes the numbers. The results come back as `Float64`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
print(lf.std().collect().to_dicts())        # sample std, ddof=1
print(lf.std(ddof=0).collect().to_dicts())  # population std, numpy-style
print(lf.var().collect().to_dicts())
print(lf.var(ddof=0).collect().to_dicts())

passed.title: with_row_count is deprecated and its column name changed to 'index'
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.with_row_count` is deprecated; use `LazyFrame.with_row_index` instead. The default column name is now `index`, not `row_nr`, so downstream code that selects `row_nr` breaks unless you pass `name='row_nr'`. The `offset` cannot be negative and raises a `ValueError`. Adding a row index can block predicate pushdown, so add it as late in the query as possible.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 3, 5]})
out = lf.with_row_index().collect()
print(out.columns)

# Keep old downstream code working by naming the column explicitly
print(lf.with_row_index("row_nr", offset=1).collect().to_dicts())

try:
    lf.with_row_index(offset=-1).collect()
except ValueError:
    print("negative offset rejected: ValueError")

passed.title: LazyFrame.unpivot uses `index`/`on`, not pandas `id_vars`/`value_vars`
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.unpivot` does not take pandas-style `id_vars=` or `value_vars=` keywords. Pass the identifier columns as `index=` and the columns to unpivot as `on=`. If `on` is omitted (`None`, the default), every column not in `index` is unpivoted; an explicitly empty `on` unpivots no columns. The output columns are named `variable` and `value` unless you set `variable_name` and `value_name`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"id": ["x", "y"], "b": [1, 3], "c": [2, 4]})

# pandas id_vars -> index, value_vars -> on
out = lf.unpivot(on=["b", "c"], index="id").sort("id", "variable").collect()
print(out.to_dicts())

# Omitting on unpivots every non-index column
all_cols = lf.unpivot(index="id", variable_name="col", value_name="val")
print(all_cols.sort("id", "col").collect().to_dicts())

The docstring confirms that `keep='any'` gives no guarantee and that `maintain_order` defaults to False, and the output shows `keep='first'` and `keep='none'` behaving as described.
The output shows nulls first for both ascending and `descending=True`, and the docstring ties stable ordering to `maintain_order`.
Every claim (unordered output, the 1.0.0 rename to `reverse`, smallest-k semantics, non-null preference) is stated in the docstring and consistent with the output.
The deprecation since 1.0.0 and the horizontal-concat replacement are in the docstring, and the output shows the null filled with the train median 0.0.
The output and docstrings confirm `ddof=1` by default, the `ddof=0` values and f64 results.
The deprecation message, the `index` default, the negative-offset ValueError and the pushdown warning are all supported by the docstrings and output.
The docstring says an empty `on` uses no columns and only `on=None` (the default) unpivots every non-index column, so 'left empty' misstates the behavior.
